title: Asia stocks roar back as Taiwan jumps 6%, Nvidia probe rattles AI trade
full_text:
Investing.com -- Asian stocks rallied on Monday, following a recovery on Wall Street, although concerns over an investigation involving Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang tempered gains as investors reassessed the outlook for the artificial intelligence trade.
The MSCI Asia Pacific index climbed 2.3%, with Japan’s Nikkei 225 advancing 3.5% and South Korea’s KOSPI rising 1.6%. Taiwan’s Taiex jumped as much as 6.4%, its biggest advance since July, while the TOPIX gained 3.4%. The rebound followed a turbulent week in which Japanese and Taiwanese equities entered bear-market territory and Samsung Electronics and SK Hynix both lost more than 16%.
A gauge of U.S. semiconductor stocks rose 4.2% late last week as investors bought beaten-down shares amid easing concerns that a Democratic-controlled Congress would impose tighter restrictions on the AI industry following the party’s sweeping midterm victories. The S&P 500 nevertheless recorded its steepest weekly decline since April 2025, while the Nasdaq 100 lost $2.3 trillion in market value on Thursday alone.
Nvidia futures initially fell as much as 1% after the company's board announced an independent investigation into reports that Huang had been targeted in a foreign intelligence operation. Huang had acknowledged being unfaithful to his wife, while the board said it had no reason to believe Nvidia secrets or U.S. national security had been compromised.
Nasdaq 100 futures were last up 0.7% and S&P 500 futures had gained 0.6%.
Taiwan leads rebound as authorities move to stabilise markets
Taiwan’s Taiex recovered from a seven-session losing streak, its longest since 2022, after the market regulator and finance ministry announced measures to restore investor confidence.
Taiwan Semiconductor Manufacturing Co. and MediaTek each climbed at least 6%, leading the rebound after the technology-heavy market entered bear territory last week.
The Financial Supervisory Commission cut the permitted volume of intraday short-selling orders using borrowed securities to 3% of a stock’s average daily trading volume over the previous 30 sessions, from 30%. It also raised the minimum margin requirement for short-selling to 130% from 90%.
Authorities said the NT$500 billion ($15.2 billion) national stock stabilisation fund remained available for deployment.
Meanwhile, Brent crude fell 0.9% to $97.44 a barrel as U.S. President Donald Trump said further strikes on Iran were unlikely if negotiations over its nuclear programme made progress.
Investors were also awaiting U.S. inflation data on Tuesday for clues on the interest-rate outlook, with markets pricing in nearly an 80% probability of a Federal Reserve rate increase by year-end.
China, India and regional markets show mixed performance
Chinese and Indian equities also attracted renewed demand as investors rotated away from AI-exposed markets. Mainland China’s CSI 300 rose 0.3% and the Shanghai Composite gained 0.5%, while India’s Nifty 50 fell 0.2%.
China's October inflation figures offered a mixed signal. Higher energy and commodity costs lifted factory-gate prices, but weak domestic demand meant many manufacturers struggled to pass those increases on to customers, squeezing margins.
Elsewhere, Hong Kong’s Hang Seng rose 0.2%, Australia’s S&P/ASX 200 and New Zealand’s NZX 50 slipped 0.2%, respectively, and Singapore’s Straits Times Index was unchanged. Indonesia’s Jakarta Composite gained 0.8%, while Malaysia’s KLCI fell 1.2%.
The Philippines’ PSEi Composite dropped 0.7% as the country’s economy expanded just 2.1% year-on-year in the third quarter, slowing from 2.4% in the second quarter and 4% in the same period last year.
ANZ Group Holdings shares fell 4.5% to A$38.62 despite the Australian lender reporting full-year cash profit of A$7.59 billion, narrowly exceeding analyst expectations. The bank also increased provisions amid a more volatile economic environment.
The latest rebound offers some relief after last week's sharp technology-led losses, but investors remain cautious about AI valuations, regulatory risks and the scale of infrastructure spending. Attention now turns to U.S. inflation data and further evidence of whether the technology sector can sustain its growth.

full_text:

The consumer price index (CPI) rose 0.7% year on year, below economists’ expectations of 0.8% and September’s 0.9% increase, data showed on Monday.
On a monthly basis, consumer prices were unchanged, compared with a 0.2% increase in September.

full_text:

HONG KONG, Nov 9 (Reuters) - Asian markets and US equity futures had an upbeat start on Monday, edging into positive territory after a wild week when tech-heavy markets in Asia suffered some of their steepest falls in years over AI.
MSCI’s broadest index of Asia-Pacific shares outside Japan rose 2% after sliding 4.6% last week. Japan’s Nikkei index added 3.5%, while Korean shares climbed 1.8%.

Global stocks had already been under pressure in recent weeks with the AI trade crumbling amid rising interest rates, and the US midterm results deepened worries about increased regulation of AI and data centres. But analysts say some dip-buyers might be emerging in a week relatively light on data and events.
"The only fundamental this week that matters is price," said Chris Weston, head of research at brokerage Pepperstone in Melbourne.
"You could easily see a lot of people going, ’You know what, now’s the time to buy — blood on the streets. It’s not as bad as everyone thinks,’" he said. "It will be driven by flow, and fundamentals will mean very little."
Earnings reports due this week from tech companies including CoreWeave, Applied Materials and Cisco Systems are set to put the profitability of AI ambitions to the test amid the massive costs of the build-out.
Meanwhile, a company-led investigation by industry bellwether Nvidia into whether its CEO Jensen Huang had been the target of a foreign spying effort could also stoke volatility, analysts said.
Nvidia shares fell about 3.5% in after-hours trading on the Blue Ocean alternative trading system, while perpetual futures declined roughly 3%, according to Hyperliquid pricing.
Brent crude fell to $98.2 per barrel after US President Donald Trump said on Sunday he was highly unlikely to order fresh attacks on Iran as long as talks to end the conflict progress.

title: Citi sees Japanese stocks gaining into year-end
full_text:
Investing.com-- Citi said Japanese equities were likely to recover toward the end of 2026, arguing that a sharp sell-off on November 6 priced in a recession it did not expect.
The brokerage said current share prices could not be justified unless the global and Japanese economies entered clearly defined recessions, starting with a pullback in U.S. AI and data center investment.
Japanese stocks fell sharply in early-November, with the Nikkei 225down over 7% so far in the month. Investors grew concerned that the U.S. midterm elections would lead to tighter regulation of AI and data center spending.
Concerns over more interest rate hikes by the Bank of Japan also weighed, after the central bank officially declared victory against deflation, opening up the door to more monetary tightening.
This saw the Japanese stock decline extend well beyond the tech sector, which Citi said pointed to expectations of a broad deterioration in the economy and corporate earnings.
Citi estimated that the earnings per share (EPS) implied by the November 6 close was roughly 20% below current consensus. That was equivalent to a decline of nearly 30% in overall Japanese EPS for fiscal 2027, it said.
Downward revisions of more than 20%, or declines of more than 30%, had been seen only during recessions, Citi said.
The market also implied a fall of more than 50% year-on-year in fiscal 2027 EPS for the tech sector, as measured by MSCI Japan IT. Citi called that pricing excessive.
Tech accounted for only about 23% of TOPIX, and Citi said it was difficult to see overall EPS falling by more than 30% even if tech earnings halved, provided other sectors held firm. It said the market was effectively pricing in sharp downgrades outside AI and semiconductor-related names, which it called a clear overreaction.
The market had priced in steep EPS cuts on several occasions, most recently during the 2025 tariff shock, Citi said. In those cases, consensus EPS tended to decline gradually while market-implied EPS improved sharply, and share prices rebounded.
Citi acknowledged that Japanese equities could remain highly volatile in the near term but maintained its main scenario of a market pick-up toward year-end.

While market chatter blamed the tech sell-off on the recent "blue sweep" in the U.S. mid-terms - sparking fears over bipartisan opposition to data center expansions - Deutsche Bank attributed the plunge primarily to a "forced positioning unwind".
Despite the grim sentiment, the bank remains aggressively bullish on the sector. Strategists reiterated an "overweight" rating on tech, arguing the recent collapse has created a highly favorable risk-reward setup and describing the market as a coiled spring.

title: China extends suspensions of 24% tariff on US goods, port fees on US ships for two months
full_text:
BEIJING, Nov 9 (Reuters) - China on Monday extended the suspension of its additional tariff of 24% on US imports and the suspension of special port fees on US-linked ships for two months.
• The 24% additional tariff on US imports will continue to be suspended for two months from 1:01 p.m. (0501 GMT) on Tuesday, but a tariff of 10% will remain, its state council, or cabinet, said
• The suspension of special port fees on US-linked vessels will be extended until January 10, 2027, China’s transport ministry said in a statement
• China is also continuing to suspend a probe into shipping and shipbuilding supply chain security, the ministry said.
• After September’s Washington summit of their leaders, both sides proposed a $60-billion package of reciprocal tariff cuts, including roughly $17 billion worth of US farm goods that China imported in 2024, though the plan has yet to be finalised
• China is extending the tariff suspensions to implement the "outcomes and consensus reached at the Washington meeting between the heads of state of China and the United States", the council’s tariffs panel said in a statement
• China has "noted that the US side has repeatedly stated that it intends to use Section 301 tariffs to replace the tariffs imposed under the International Emergency Economic Powers Act (IEEPA) that have been held invalid by judicial rulings" it said
• China will "closely follow subsequent measures taken by the US side and will, as appropriate, adjust relevant tariff countermeasures in light of developments," it added
• Continued suspension of some additional tariffs on U.S. goods will help ensure a stable and predictable policy environment for ties and promote development of China–U.S. economic and trade relations, it said

title: NextDC pauses uncontracted projects after Australian data centre woes
full_text:
By Christine Chen
SYDNEY, Nov 9 (Reuters) - Australian data centre operator NextDC said on Monday it would stop work on all projects without customer contracts following a big setback on a facility in Melbourne, as two major rivals finalised buying an A$715 million ($492 million) stake in the company.
A suspension of work on its flagship M3 data centre expansion in Melbourne due to power delays and community backlash forced the company to cut its earnings forecasts last month, sending its share price tumbling 42%.
The decision to pause uncontracted projects after the Melbourne delay is another blow for NextDC, which had been touted as Australia’s most prolific data centre developer.
"The last couple of weeks (I) certainly didn’t expect to be in the position we’re in today having to deal with some delays," NextDC’s chief executive, Craig Scroggie, told the UBS Australasia conference.
"That’s unfortunately probably reflective of the global environment in relation to the engagement, social license, people’s feelings about artificial intelligence and data centres being the physical embodiment of that."
Scroggie said the M3 delay meant the top priority was to win community backing for that project and "anything that didn’t have a customer contract and a customer commitment that we absolutely have to deliver on is now no longer a priority."
He did not say how many projects would be paused. The company had 11 centres in development or in the planning stages, according to its 2026 annual report.
"That work can’t restart until we clearly communicate that we’ve solved this problem, that we’ve earned the trust of everybody that’s been supporting us, and then we will get back to work."
NextDC’s rivals Goodman Group and its New York-listed partner, Digital Realty, bought a 9.9% stake in the company last week following the share price plunge.
"When you have a challenge like we’ve had in the last couple of weeks, it’s not really any surprise to me that people ... look at that and say, now might be the time," Scroggie said.
Goodman and Digital Realty said they had no plans at the moment to launch a takeover offer, but reserved the right to do so. They said they would "look forward to a potential collaboration with the NextDC board and management on the ways and forms in which the parties may help to address the challenges facing the company".
Following their share raid, NextDC’s share price recovered the ground lost from the earnings writedown.

title: Take Five: Tech wreck and roll
full_text:
Nov 9 (Reuters) - Traders on the world’s financial markets go into the week hoping the storm engulfing tech stocks blows itself out and for no new escalation in the Iran war that sends oil prices surging again.
There are also key US and Chinese data, the UN’s COP climate summit gets underway in Turkey, horse trading begins over the next ECB chief and New Zealand is in limbo after an inconclusive weekend election.
Here’s all you need to know about the coming week in markets by Dhara Ranasinghe, Alun John and Simon Jessop in London, Lewis Krauskopf in New York and Gregor Stuart Hunter in Singapore.
1/ HOUSE OF P-AI-N
The Democrats’ US midterm win has been the latest hammer blow to the once-unstoppable Big Tech trade.
The Nasdaq’s 5.5% slump on Thursday was its biggest since the Liberation Day rout of April 2025 and wiped $2.5 trillion off that one index alone.
Worries had already been intensifying about the stratospheric cost of the AI buildout. Now, post-midterms, the prospect of tougher regulations that slow everything down is hurting just as much.
Democratic wins in Texas and Georgia reflected the voter backlash against the data centres that are at the heart of the AI boom, but are also ugly and loud and require huge amounts of energy and water.
Some sense a compromise might be struck since AI has become a key economic driver. But if the rout resumes next week, growth worries will likely mount and plenty will be wondering whether something somewhere in the financial system tied to it all might break.
2/KEEPING A CLOSE CPI
US data and the direction of oil prices over the week could determine whether the Federal Reserve hikes its interest rates one more time before the year is out.
Tuesday’s US consumer price index (CPI) — perhaps the most closely watched inflation measure — is expected to show a monthly rise of 0.3%, according to a Reuters poll, while Friday brings another key read on producer prices.
As it stands, traders are pricing in a more than 80% chance of a Fed hike at its December 8-9 meeting. That would take the federal funds rate — the primary driver of global borrowing costs — to 4.00%-4.25% and follow the Fed’s first rise in three years back in September.
Then there’s oil. Crude prices have dropped 18% since the Republicans’ hammering in the US midterms stoked bets that President Donald Trump may look to de-escalate the Iran war. Over the weekend, the US President downplayed the likelihood of fresh attacks - as long as peace talks progress.
3/WHO’S IT GOING TO EC-BE?
European economic growth has been surprisingly resilient this year in the face of sky-high energy prices and rising borrowing costs.
The coming week will provide another test with quarterly employment data due, as well as a more refined estimate of quarterly GDP. Last month’s preliminary flash Q3 reading showed 0.4% growth.
If confirmed, it will boost the mood at Monday’s gathering of euro zone finance ministers, where another top topic will be who replaces European Central Bank President Christine Lagarde when she leaves Frankfurt in February.
Nominations have now been finalised. The two candidates are former Dutch central bank governor Klaas Knot and Spain’s Pablo Hernandez de Cos, the head of the Bank for International Settlements.
The EU hopes to appoint a new ECB president by its mid-December summit, so it will have to get a move on. Monday’s meeting could be busy.
4/COP SHOW
The UN’s COP31 climate summit kicks off in Turkey on Monday, with more than 80 world leaders expected to attend against the backdrop of worsening extreme weather events that have caused a slew of devastating disasters this year.
With the US not formally involved under climate-sceptic Donald Trump, his humbling in this week’s midterms will be a glimmer of hope for some, although efforts to build coalitions of the willing to phase out fossil fuels and halt deforestation will need to continue.
As the Middle East war keeps oil and gas prices high, host Turkey is also pushing nations to accelerate the shift to green power so that 35% of the world’s power comes from electricity by 2035, from around 23% now.
Overhanging everything, though, will be the thorny issue of money. With development aid getting slashed by many richer countries, vulnerable developing countries will once again be looking for more help to cope with climate change.
5/THRILLER IN MANILA
There will be a flurry of last-minute diplomacy in Manila next week as senior government officials start the final preparations on Friday for the following week’s ASEAN nations summit.
Philippine President Ferdinand Marcos Jr, who is hosting the November 15-17 gathering, has said Chinese Premier Li Qiang will be there, while both President Trump and his Canadian sparring partner, Prime Minister Mark Carney, are expected to attend too.
Indonesia is also likely to come under pressure for its wildfires that blanketed much of the region in thick smog earlier this year, with Singapore already vowing to strengthen an agreement on transboundary haze.
Elsewhere in Asia, Chinese inflation data has just seen producer prices notch their fastest increase in nearly 4-1/2 years, trade figures are due on Tuesday, followed by lending data later in the week.
New Zealand, meanwhile, faces weeks of uncertainty after its weekend election produced no clear winner.

title: Nvidia’s shares slide as chip giant probes CEO over spy claims
full_text:
By Heekyong Yang, Kyu-seok Shim and Tom Westbrook
SEOUL/SYDNEY, Nov 9 (Reuters) - Nvidia shares fell sharply on Monday after an internal investigation into whether CEO Jensen Huang had been targeted by a foreign intelligence effort put his future at the AI chipmaker under scrutiny.
The internal probe followed a media report that Huang had a close relationship with a Chinese businesswoman who allegedly passed information to Beijing. Huang told Nvidia’s employees that he had been unfaithful to his wife, without disclosing details of the relationship.
The investigation, announced on Sunday, has put a spotlight on Huang’s future given Nvidia’s status as the world’s most valuable chipmaker and the CEO’s role as the most prolific salesman of the AI boom.
The leather-jacketed Huang enjoys rock-star status worldwide, particularly in Asia, where he often mingles freely with fans, taking selfies and signing autographs for his devoted followers.
The fallout from the probe extended to South Korea, where Madison Huang, Huang’s daughter and an Nvidia executive, cancelled a planned visit to Seoul for an Nvidia conference that was set to begin on Monday, according to companies she had been scheduled to meet.
Nvidia’s shares tumbled more than 6% in Frankfurt trading, extending last week’s selloff and pushing the stock to fresh multi-month lows. At those levels, the chipmaker stood to lose about $270 billion from its closing price on Friday, according to LSEG Datastream.
"The market’s probably telling you now this does no favours to the stock whatsoever in a time when there’s a lot of conjecture as to the build-out of data centres," said Chris Weston, head of research at brokerage Pepperstone in Melbourne.
But Weston said he did not think Huang, whom he described as the "godfather of AI", would be replaced.
"If we genuinely thought he was going to step down ... the stock would be down — it would be an absolute bloodbath, to be honest,” he said.
The New York Times reported last month that Huang had a relationship with Alice Huang, an unrelated former executive of Singapore-based company Megaspeed, who US authorities investigated and concluded was a Chinese intelligence asset.
"The so-called Chinese spy narrative is purely a groundless accusation, slander, and a smear," Chinese Foreign Ministry spokesperson Guo Jiakun told reporters in Beijing.
Megaspeed did not respond immediately to a request for comment on Monday, a public holiday in Singapore.
Alice Huang did not respond to the New York Times last month when it first reported her relationship with Huang, and Reuters could not determine her location to seek comment on Monday.

title: COP31 summit leaders urge world to "move faster" on climate
full_text:
By Valerie Volcovici and Simon Jessop
ANTALYA, Turkey, Nov 9 (Reuters) - Leaders of the COP31 climate summit urged the world to accelerate the fight against global warming as rising temperatures and an increasing number of climate-driven disasters threaten lives and the global economy, as the annual meeting began in Turkey on Monday.
The comments at the start of the two-week UN conference were an appeal to governments to focus on climate, even as other international crises from war to soaring inflation and the uncertainty of AI compete for their attention.
"The urgency of this moment must drive us forward," UN Climate Change Executive Secretary Simon Stiell said in prepared remarks for the opening of the event on Turkey’s Mediterranean coast, adding that progress so far was "nowhere near fast enough."
A report by the United Nations Environment Programme published in October said the world was already set to overshoot 1.5C of warming above pre-industrial times, the threshold set at the 2015 Paris climate summit to avoid the worst consequences of warming.
This year is on track to be one of the four hottest on record, driven by a powerful El Niño, a UN report showed on Monday. 2026 has also stood out with a series of extreme heatwaves across Western Europe and a glacier collapse in Nepal that triggered a catastrophic flood killing more than 1,450 people, with thousands still missing.
Turkey’s COP31 presidency has focused this year’s summit on a goal to electrify more than a third of the global economy by 2035, up from around a fifth today. It is asking nations to sign onto a pledge supporting that target.
Theoretically, such a goal could help reduce planet-warming emissions by speeding the global shift away from fossil fuel-powered vehicles, furnaces, boilers, cooking stoves, and other greenhouse gas-emitting equipment.
"We want people to feel the results of climate talks in daily life: in buildings that use less energy, in clean public transport, in energy they can afford and in new jobs," Turkey’s COP31 President Murat Kurum said in prepared remarks.
But climate advocates have criticised the pledge because it does not require the additional electricity to come from low-carbon sources, setting up an early fight over whether electrification alone should count as climate progress.
WAR AND TECH
The Iran war has underscored the world’s attachment to fossil fuels, as has Russia’s invasion of Ukraine and the ensuing sanctions on Moscow’s energy exports, though some say the wars have also shown the benefits of moving to renewables.
The Iran war, now in its ninth month, severely disrupted Middle East oil shipments through the Strait of Hormuz, lifting fuel prices around the globe and prompting a scramble for new supplies.
US President Donald Trump’s administration — which is shunning climate talks for the second year running — has encouraged policies maximising oil, gas, and coal production to address the Mideast disruptions.
South Korea, India, Thailand and other Asian nations, meanwhile, have also increased their reliance on coal or taken steps to boost coal-fired power generation.
"A lot of people who previously might have been embarrassed to argue for continuing very high use of fossil fuel are now feeling empowered to make that case," said John Holdren of Harvard University, who was a science adviser to Barack Obama when he was US president.
At the same time, the deployment of renewable energy has also risen, driven by surging exports of cheap clean tech from China, cheering advocates for ambitious climate action.
Stiell told the summit renewables were the clear answer to improving energy security.
"This year’s fossil fuel cost chaos has delivered a global shockwave, hitting households hard and spreading inflation like a cancer," he said.
"But the solutions are clear," he added, saying renewable energy installations had saved the global economy hundreds of billions of dollars.
The rapid rollout of AI is also complicating talks, driving a surge in global power demand and contributing to rising greenhouse gas emissions.
Turkey will call on governments, businesses and other institutions at COP31 to sign a pledge outlining principles to ensure AI is developed and deployed sustainably.
Chris Bowen, Australia’s president of COP31 negotiations, said he hoped the conference would show the world that multilateralism works.
"Paris is working," he said, referring to the landmark 2015 deal to limit global warming. "But we must move faster."

title: Google expands AI chip lineup as Nvidia faces CEO spy scandal
full_text:
Investing.com -- Alphabet Inc.’s Google is expanding its artificial intelligence chip portfolio, stepping up its challenge to Nvidia Corp. just as a controversy involving Nvidia Chief Executive Jensen Huang adds another source of uncertainty for the market leader.
Google is introducing two new variations of its tensor processing units, or TPUs, designed to address growing demand for confidential computing and AI applications that need to process larger amounts of information, Bloomberg News reported Monday.
The new TPU 8tx and 8i Max offerings are designed for different workloads, reflecting Google’s view that the next phase of artificial intelligence will require increasingly specialized hardware.
The TPU 8tx targets secure, confidential computing, with potential applications among government agencies and companies operating in regulated industries. The system also incorporates chips from Advanced Micro Devices Inc., as part of a collaboration between the two companies.
The 8i Max, meanwhile, is designed to run AI applications requiring longer context windows, allowing models to consider substantially more information when responding to queries. Such capabilities are particularly relevant for drug discovery, mathematical applications and coding tools.
Neither offering represents an entirely new silicon design. Instead, Google has reconfigured its existing hardware to address specific requirements emerging from customers, according to Bloomberg.
"This really follows the thesis that we have here at Google, which is that the future is going to be about specialization, and the upsides for specialization continue to be significant," Google chip chief Amin Vahdat told Bloomberg.
The announcement marks an acceleration in Google’s chip development. The company previously introduced a new generation of AI processors roughly every two years, but this year unveiled two generations of specialized processors simultaneously, with the latest variations expanding the lineup further.
Google gains ground as Nvidia faces fresh uncertainty
The timing is notable for the semiconductor industry, where Nvidia’s dominance is facing increasing competition from companies developing their own AI accelerators.
Google has emerged as one of the most credible challengers, benefiting from years of internal chip development and growing interest from AI developers seeking alternatives to Nvidia’s processors.
The opportunity extends beyond Google’s own AI operations. Demand for computing capacity remains substantial, while the emergence of AI agents is creating new requirements for inference, memory and security. Specialized processors could allow customers to optimize performance and costs for particular workloads rather than relying on general-purpose solutions.
Nvidia, meanwhile, continues to benefit from demand that exceeds available supply, leaving considerable room for competitors to establish businesses without necessarily displacing the market leader.
But the company faces a separate challenge Monday following reports that Huang may have been targeted by a Chinese intelligence operation.
Nvidia’s board announced Sunday that it would launch an independent investigation into reports that Huang had been the target of a foreign intelligence effort. The announcement followed a report concerning his relationship with a business executive whom US authorities reportedly suspected of gathering information for Beijing.
Huang also acknowledged being unfaithful to his wife in a message to employees, apologizing to his family and colleagues.
Nvidia said its board had no reason to believe that national security or company secrets had been compromised and expressed confidence in Huang’s leadership. The CEO has pledged to cooperate with the investigation.
The controversy is weighing on Nvidia shares, which were down 5.70% Monday, while Alphabet shares were up 2.4%.
The divergence reflects two separate developments: Google’s expanding ambitions in AI infrastructure and the unexpected leadership and reputational uncertainty confronting Nvidia.
For Alphabet, the latest TPU expansion strengthens its position in a market that could become increasingly fragmented as AI workloads evolve. For Nvidia, the immediate concern is less about losing its technological lead overnight than maintaining investor confidence in a business whose extraordinary growth has been closely associated with Huang’s leadership.
Google still has a considerable distance to travel before matching Nvidia’s scale and software ecosystem. But its latest move underscores that competition in AI semiconductors is increasingly about offering the right processor for each task, rather than simply producing the most powerful chip.

title: BofA downgrades 3 European chip stocks on high memory exposure
full_text:
Investing.com - Bank of America has downgraded three European semiconductor stocks in a single sweep, cutting VAT Group to Neutral from Buy, Comet to Underperform from Buy, and Inficon to Underperform from Neutral, warning that high memory exposure leaves all three vulnerable if the chip cycle turns.
The moves follow BofA's downgrade of Siltronic to Underperform in the prior week, bringing the firm's tally of recent European semis cuts to four names. Accordingly, a deteriorating memory cycle has historically hit high-fixed-cost equipment suppliers hardest, and BofA judges VAT and Comex no longer warrant Buy ratings.
"Rarely has the market been as polarised between universally bullish bottom-up indicators and bearish top-down indicators," the firm's analyst wrote.
Company-level order books and management commentary across European semicap names remain constructive, yet BofA sees mounting macro-level threats: potential financing stress for so-called neoclouds and tightening regulatory scrutiny of data-center buildouts.
U.S. cloud capital expenditure is currently running at a $300 billion per quarter rate ($1.2 trillion annualized), heading toward $375 billion per quarter in calendar 2027.
However, BofA calculates that if the current rate marks an intermediate peak, that implies roughly 20% potential downside versus CY27 capex expectations — equivalent, by its math, to a roughly 10 GW headwind against its 40-plus GW baseline deployment assumption for 2027 data centers (using a $40 billion per GW capex average across merchant and custom chips).
On the valuation front, the Philadelphia Semiconductor Index (SOX) has underperformed the S&P 500 by more than 37% since its June peak, which BofA identifies as the largest such relative drawdown in the past 20 years.
That dislocation has pushed European semicap stocks to roughly 10x EV/EBIT turns below their median multiples on CY27 consensus estimates, while EU analog names trade 1.6x turns below their medians, per BofA.
Yet the firm is not broadly bearish. BofA retains Buy ratings on ASML, ASM International, and BE Semiconductor's peer TPRO, noting all three trade 0.5x to 4.0x below their five-year historical EV/EBIT multiples.
"Given the exceptionally strong demand backdrop for WFE, we think the risk/reward is positively skewed and maintain our Buy ratings," the firm's analyst said.
On the other end of the valuation spectrum, BofA flags BESI, Mycronic, and Inficon as trading approximately 5.0x above their historical trough EV/EBIT multiples, making them more vulnerable to further de-rating.
Among analog names, Infineon, Tower Semiconductor, and Melexis trade closest to trough multiples, while STMicro, AMS Osram, and Nordic Semiconductor sit furthest above them.
"STMicro, AMS Osram and Nordic trade the most above their trough multiples largely because of their greater consumer exposure, which could make them beneficiaries of a rotation out of AI, in our view," the analyst added.
"While timing a top in the sector is difficult, we think there are enough warning signs to warrant a more selective approach to the sector," BofA wrote, adding that "it is more prudent to own the stocks with the best idiosyncratic drivers rather than have a broad exposure to the semiconductor cycle."

title: Explainer-What we know about Nvidia’s probe into CEO Jensen Huang
full_text:
Nov 9 (Reuters) - Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang faces a board probe into whether he was the target of a foreign intelligence effort after a media report linked him to a Chinese businesswoman accused of passing information to Beijing.
The New York Times reported last month that Huang had a relationship with Alice Huang, an unrelated former executive of Singapore-based company Megaspeed, who US authorities investigated and concluded was a Chinese intelligence asset.
Here is what is known about Huang’s background and his pivotal role at chipmaker Nvidia as well as the US scrutiny of Megaspeed and Alice Huang.
WHO IS JENSEN HUANG?
Huang, 63, co-founded Nvidia in 1993 with Chris Malachowsky and Curtis Priem and has led the company ever since, making him one of Silicon Valley’s longest-serving founder CEOs.
Born in Taiwan and raised in the US, Huang became one of the most powerful figures in the AI revolution as he transformed Nvidia from a maker of video-game graphics chips into the world’s dominant supplier of AI processors.
His trademark leather jackets and high-profile product launches have made him one of the few corporate leaders in the world synonymous with their companies.
Huang has been married for decades to Lori Huang, whom he met while studying engineering. The couple have two children who both work at Nvidia.
Their daughter Madison Huang is a senior director of product and technical marketing for physical AI platforms at Nvidia, while their son Spencer Huang manages robotics software products.
Huang said on Sunday in a message to employees that he had been unfaithful to his wife and took "full responsibility" for his actions.
WHAT DOES NVIDIA DO?
Nvidia’s chip designs have been at the heart of major technology trends from video games to self-driving cars to cloud computing and AI.
Under Huang’s leadership, the company bet early on AI, and when ChatGPT launched in late 2022, Nvidia’s chips were already positioned at the center of a surge in demand for AI computing.
Nvidia has become one of the world’s most valuable businesses and a critical supplier to major technology firms, with its valuation surging from $420 billion in late 2022 to $4.5 trillion as of November 6.
WHO IS ALICE HUANG AND WHAT IS MEGASPEED?
The US has been investigating Megaspeed, a Singapore-based cloud computing firm and an Nvidia customer, over suspicions that it helped Beijing gain access to Nvidia’s advanced AI chips that are barred from shipment to China.
The New York Times last month reported that Alice Huang, a Chinese citizen, had developed a close relationship with the Nvidia boss and allegedly fed information directly to Beijing.
Reuters could not independently verify the claims made in the report, nor could it verify Alice Huang’s current employment status with Megaspeed.
According to its website, Megaspeed is an Nvidia Cloud Partner in the Asia-Pacific region, with Nvidia’s GB200 NVL72 and HGX H100 chips on offer.
Megaspeed did not respond immediately to a request for comment on Monday, a public holiday in Singapore.
Alice Huang did not respond to the New York Times last month when it first reported her relationship with Huang, and Reuters could not determine her location to seek comment on Monday.
WHAT NATIONAL SECURITY ISSUES COULD BE INVOLVED?
Nvidia sits at the center of the technological rivalry between the United States and China. Washington has imposed restrictions on exports of advanced AI chips to China since 2022.
The controversy over Huang’s contacts with Alice Huang comes at a vulnerable time for Nvidia. Investors are already fretting about the sustainability of the AI boom that helped drive the company’s rise. The board probe raises fresh questions about the future of the executive most closely associated with its success.
Senior Republicans in the US House of Representatives have already sought briefings from Huang following the New York Times report, citing national security concerns.
Nvidia has said its board has "no reason to believe" US national security or company secrets were affected, though an independent committee of directors will review all available information.
HOW WILL NVIDIA CONDUCT ITS PROBE?
The company said a committee of independent directors, assisted by outside independent counsel, will oversee the investigation.
Huang fully supports the review and has committed to cooperating with it, Nvidia said in a statement.

title: Goodyear Tire stock falls 7% as CEO Mark Stewart exits abruptly
full_text:
Investing.com -- Goodyear Tire & Rubber Company (NASDAQ) shares fell 7% Monday after Chief Executive Officer and President Mark Stewart stepped down from his positions and the company’s board of directors, effective immediately, in an unexpected leadership change amid an ongoing strategic review.
The company announced Monday that Roger Wood, a current board member, has been appointed interim CEO. Wood will lead Goodyear while the board conducts a search for a permanent successor with the assistance of an executive search firm.
The departure comes as Goodyear struggles to restore profitability, adding uncertainty around the company’s turnaround efforts. Last week, the tiremaker reported a third-quarter net loss of $238 million, while adjusted results showed a loss of $0.11 per share, compared with earnings of $0.28 per share a year earlier. Net sales fell 2.3% to $4.5 billion, while tire unit volumes declined 3.3%.
Goodyear has also faced pressure from weaker replacement-tire demand, higher manufacturing costs and inflation.
A special committee of the board, formed earlier this year, has been conducting a strategic review of the company’s businesses and operations, focused on identifying opportunities to strengthen performance and create shareholder value.
The board is evaluating a broad range of strategic and operational initiatives, including further optimizing Goodyear’s business mix and manufacturing footprint, improving efficiency, and investing in new products and capabilities to support long-term growth. The company did not provide a timetable for the review or indicate what specific measures might emerge.

title: Nvidia intervention preceded transfer of chip probe to Justice Department
full_text:
Investing.com -- Nvidia’s efforts to communicate with U.S. officials over a suspected chip-smuggling investigation preceded an unusual decision to transfer the case from the Commerce Department to the Justice Department, raising new questions about the company’s influence over export-control enforcement.
According to a New York Times report published Monday, Nvidia General Counsel Tim Teter contacted Commerce Department investigators in August 2025 seeking information about an investigation into Megaspeed, a Singapore-based data center company suspected of diverting advanced Nvidia AI chips to China.
In his email, Teter said senior Commerce official Jeff Kessler had given him permission to contact the investigators. The officials were reportedly alarmed by the reference to Kessler, who oversees the department’s export-control operations and reports directly to Commerce Secretary Howard Lutnick.
The investigators declined Nvidia’s request for a meeting. After receiving the email chain, Kessler instructed them to continue handling the case strictly by the book. He did not direct investigators to share information with Nvidia or intervene in their investigative decisions, according to a Commerce Department official cited by the Times.
The episode nevertheless prompted internal discussions at Commerce, with officials raising concerns that the department’s interactions with Nvidia could compromise the investigation. The Justice Department subsequently requested that Commerce suspend its work and transfer the case, according to people familiar with the matter.
The Justice Department is now conducting a criminal investigation into Megaspeed. The transfer was particularly unusual because Commerce investigators had spent months building the case and could potentially have pursued administrative action to restrict the company’s access to U.S. technology.
Megaspeed had imported billions of dollars’ worth of Nvidia AI equipment into Malaysia while developing data centers across Southeast Asia to serve Chinese clients, including Alibaba. Although operating data centers for Chinese customers is not itself illegal, U.S. authorities suspected that some of the chips were being illegally rerouted into China.
The case is attracting renewed attention following revelations that Megaspeed executive Alice Huang, who reportedly had a personal relationship with Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang, was believed by U.S. intelligence officials to be working for the Chinese government. Nvidia announced Sunday that its board was investigating Jensen Huang’s relationship with the executive.
The latest report adds a separate dimension to the controversy: how Nvidia communicated with officials overseeing an investigation involving its own technology, and whether those interactions affected the government’s enforcement process.
The Times also reported that the Commerce Department has not added a company to its Entity List in more than a year, the longest such stretch in 18 years. The list is a key U.S. mechanism for restricting foreign companies’ access to American technology.
Nvidia has defended its engagement with government officials, saying it regularly provides information gathered from the field, requests guidance and works with authorities to stop suspected chip smuggling while preserving lawful sales.
There is no evidence in the report that Kessler ordered investigators to halt their work or that Nvidia successfully influenced the outcome. The Justice Department’s ongoing criminal investigation means the case has not been dropped.

title: Tech set to still sway US stock market’s course despite AI-driven swoon
full_text:
By Lewis Krauskopf
NEW YORK, Nov 9 (Reuters) - Even with the steep pullback in AI names, the US stock market is poised to rely on the performance of technology shares — and investors are on guard for obstacles that could trip up the trade in the coming weeks.
A month-long swoon in technology and AI-related stocks culminated this week in the biggest one-day drop for the S&P 500 technology sector in over six years. Investors are concerned Democratic victories in the midterm elections would lead to slower data-center spending that has been at the heart of the market’s rally.
Yet even with the drop, tech remains by far the biggest sector in the S&P 500, the benchmark index for the US stock market. Although its sway has diminished modestly, the tech sector still held a greater than 35% weight in the S&P 500 as of Thursday’s close.
"Because so much of technology is AI-sensitive, it’s going to have an impact on the entire sector, and that sector carries so much weight within the S&P 500," said Robert Pavlik, senior portfolio manager at Dakota Wealth Management. "So weakness in AI is going to drag down tech, which drags down the S&P 500."
The sector’s percentage of S&P 500 market capitalization remains above the level it reached during the height of the Internet bubble era in 2000.
The tech sector alone does not fully capture AI’s influence. For example, three hyperscalers spending massively on data centers — Alphabet, Amazon and Meta Platforms — are classified in other sectors.
The continued heavy weighting of technology is a byproduct of the huge gains for the sector during the US stock bull market that began in October 2022. Even with the tech sector’s latest slide, it has gained more than 200% over that period, nearly double the S&P 500’s gain.
Some of the biggest AI winners are still logging significant year-to-date gains despite their recent slides. For example, shares of Sandisk remained up about 250% in 2026, while Dell Technologies was last up about 160% and Micron Technology had gained 140%.
As stocks rebounded somewhat on Friday, the S&P 500 was last up nearly 8% for the year, with the tech sector up about 11%.
"If somebody is in a profit-taking mode, there are still profits to be had," said Chuck Carlson, CEO at Horizon Investment Services.
The slide in tech has also made valuations for the stocks appear — at least on the surface — more modest. The tech sector’s forward price-to-earnings ratio — based on earnings estimates for the next 12 months — fell to 17.1 as of Thursday, according to LSEG Datastream, after it rose above 32 in October 2025.
The P/E ratio for the overall S&P 500 stood at 17.9. This week marked the first time since 2017 that the tech sector’s P/E has fallen below that of the broader market.
The drop in valuations means "arguably ... the market is already pricing in a lot of bad news," said Keith Lerner, chief investment officer at Truist Advisory Services.
"We are moving toward a situation where a little good news could go a long way," Lerner said in a note on Thursday.
Investors will be watching a number of potential catalysts in the coming weeks that could drive the AI trade in one direction or the other:
** ANTHROPIC IPO: Developments with the initial public offering of AI lab Anthropic are poised to drive sentiment about the AI trade. Reuters reported on Thursday that potential investors are raising doubts about whether the company can proceed with its IPO roadshow next week in time for a November listing. The discussions reflect in part the impact of the sharp tech stock swoon.
** TECH EARNINGS: While the bulk of third-quarter earnings reports have finished, some key results remain. Cloud company CoreWeave, which has been at the center of concerns about financing the AI buildout, reports on Tuesday. AI bellwether Nvidia is due on November 17, while Dell reports on November 24.
** MACRO BACKDROP: Developments involving the US-Israeli war with Iran are set to sway stocks broadly. Expectations that the shift in Congress could bring about the end to the conflict helped drive oil prices lower this week, which in turn helped stocks. But investors are wary of an escalation in tensions with the midterms finished. Investors are also closely watching the path for interest rates and how significantly the Federal Reserve will raise rates in the coming months to tamp down inflation. One test comes with next week’s Consumer Price Index report.

Applied to Nvidia’s market capitalisation at Friday’s close, that 4% average implies roughly $185 billion in erased value — more than McDonald’s entire market cap when it fired its own CEO in 2019, per an AOL/Yahoo Finance analysis.
The historical record is consistent but not uniform. Intel (NASDAQ:INTC) fell 2.4% on the first trading day after CEO Brian Krzanich resigned on June 21, 2018, over a past consensual relationship with an employee; six months later it had lost 14.8%, trailing the S&P 500 by 4.4 percentage points over that window, according to 247wallst.com. McDonald’s (NYSE:MCD) dropped 2.7% on the first day after CEO Steve Easterbrook’s departure was announced, eventually falling 5.8% over six months, though it outperformed an S&P 500 that was hammered by COVID-19 during that period. HP’s Mark Hurd was ousted in 2010 after submitting inaccurate expense reports to conceal a personal relationship, making him the third major CEO-conduct precedent cited today; HP reached roughly 1% of S&P 500 weight at the time, the same threshold Intel hit in 2018, per AOL reporting. Nvidia, by contrast, represents approximately seven times that threshold in the index.
Scale is the critical variable separating this episode from prior precedents. No earlier scandal-hit company made up more than about 1% of the S&P 500. Nvidia’s current weight means that any sustained selloff creates forced-selling dynamics for passive and benchmark-sensitive funds in a way that Intel or McDonald’s never could.
The espionage layer is drawing political attention that prior affairs-only cases never attracted. title: Trump administration’s embrace of "perp" futures sets off risk alarms for Wall Street stalwarts
full_text:
By Laura Matthews and Hannah Lang
NEW YORK, November 9 (Reuters) - The Trump administration’s push to bring novel offshore perpetual futures to the US is raising alarms, according to interviews with four executives at incumbent exchanges and other key market participants who warned that the products will introduce serious new risks to the multitrillion-dollar derivatives market.
Pioneered in non-US crypto markets, perpetual futures, or "perps," trade around the clock and do not expire, meaning investors can hold positions indefinitely. They are usually leveraged, sometimes by as much as 50 times, and are predominantly traded by retail or individual investors.
Crypto perps trading volume reached $61.7 trillion in 2025, up 29% from 2024, according to data provider CryptoQuant, with much of that on big platforms such as Binance and Hyperliquid and based in Asia.
The Reuters interviews with executives at exchanges, trading firms, asset managers and market-structure providers revealed broader concerns that improperly regulated perps and 24-hour trading could disrupt market structure and erode risk-management safeguards bolstered after the 2007-09 financial crisis.
Traditional Wall Street exchanges were alarmed by the US Commodity Futures Trading Commission’s decision in May to formally approve US-listed crypto perps, with Kalshi, Coinbase, Robinhood and other financial technology firms jumping into the new market.
Last week, the government regulator also approved single-stock equity perps. CFTC Chair Michael Selig has said it is important to maintain US oversight of the nascent market to protect American investors.
TENSION BETWEEN ADMINISTRATION, STREET
CME Group, the big futures market operator, is suing the CFTC to overturn its May decision, arguing it has wrongly classified perps as futures, creating unfair competition and downplaying their risks. A group representing Cboe Global Markets and Citadel Securities also sued last week to reverse the CFTC’s recent equity perp approval on the same grounds.
"I think they’ve muddied the waters here significantly," said Terry Duffy, CME’s chief executive and a 40-plus-year industry veteran. "Anytime you have ambiguity in markets ... that could hurt the business."
The CFTC declined to comment on the concerns raised in the interviews. It has previously said the CME had chosen "lawfare" over competing in the new market.
The clash is the latest sign that the administration’s support for crypto and prediction markets, where some of the leading companies also run new exchanges, is fueling tensions with traditional Wall Street firms.
The standoff over market risks could grow next year when Democrats, propelled by midterm elections this week that handed them control of Congress, are likely to square off against President Donald Trump and step up oversight of the young industries.
"Many of these incumbents haven’t faced this type of disruption for a very long time," said Chris Perkins, head of crypto at Franklin Templeton.
EXCHANGES SAY PERPS ARE SWAPS, NOT FUTURES
The CFTC’s May decision sent exchange shares tumbling on competition fears. They have since recovered and executives have said they do not view perps as a serious threat to their predominantly institutional businesses.
Their chief concern is that treating perps as futures gives retail investors access to the novel products under a regulatory regime they say provides insufficient safeguards against leverage and counterparty risk. They argue the products are more akin to swaps, which face tougher margin, capital and reporting requirements and are generally less accessible to retail investors.
Traditional futures let counterparties lock in a transaction price for a later date, while swaps involve counterparties periodically exchanging cash flows or liabilities based on a benchmark. Because perps do not expire and involve ongoing funding payments between counterparties, they meet the 2010 Dodd-Frank Act’s definition of a swap, exchanges say.
In public legal notes, derivatives attorneys have said the CME has raised legitimate issues. The CFTC has said perps have futures-like features and their funding mechanism is a substitute for expiration.
"The industry is at an inflection point where product classification risks becoming a competitive tool," said Rob Hocking, global head of derivatives at Cboe, adding that the development is bad for markets.
"There needs to be a resolution in short order."
MISCLASSIFICATION, 24/7 TRADING SEEN AS RISKY
Futures-style margin requirements may be inadequate for products that behave more like swaps, increasing counterparty and liquidity risks during intense volatility, the executives said.
Mechanisms that automatically liquidate traders’ perp positions when their margin falls below required levels could amplify such stress, some said. Last year, such mechanisms triggered the biggest ever liquidation of bitcoin positions, amplifying the selloff.
The CFTC, in an advisory to futures commission merchants, has emphasized the need for enhanced customer disclosures about auto-liquidation features during extended trading hours.
The upstart platforms, meanwhile, are pushing to extend the products into other assets. Some of their executives say that without a workable US framework, the market will continue to flourish overseas and take US investors and funds with it.
"I think it’s better for those products to trade transparently inside the US regulatory perimeter than for that activity to remain offshore," said Andy Ross, Kalshi’s head of institutional business.
Some industry executives also say that perps pose market-structure risks. Because they trade continuously, the products require exchanges, clearing houses, brokers and traders to manage positions and meet margin calls around the clock.
That may work in smaller, pre-funded crypto markets, executives said, but it becomes more complex in larger markets where participants must move a lot of cash and collateral outside standard banking hours.
The CME last month said that it had shelved its proposed 24/7 crude oil futures contract mainly because commercial clients were unwilling to staff weekend trading desks.
"The traditional financial market infrastructure in the US is not yet fully equipped for true 24/7 markets," said Thomas Restout, chief executive of B2C2, an institutional crypto market maker.

Dozens of patients have initiated litigation against Novo Nordisk and Eli Lilly alleging drug-induced vision impairment, while four patients in Denmark were awarded compensation last year for developing the optic nerve condition.

title: Court blocks California from enforcing climate disclosure laws
full_text:
By Jonathan Stempel
Nov 9 (Reuters) - A federal appeals court dealt a setback to California’s desire to enforce its first-of-its-kind climate disclosure laws, blocking the state from requiring large companies to disclose climate-related financial risks and "indirect" greenhouse gas emissions.
Monday’s decision by a three-judge panel of the 9th US Circuit Court of Appeals in San Francisco is a partial victory for the US Chamber of Commerce, the American Farm Bureau Federation and several California business groups that sued to block the two state laws.
The panel said California could enforce provisions of a second law requiring large companies to report their own greenhouse emissions, and emissions from energy they buy and consume.
Democratic Governor Gavin Newsom signed both laws in 2023, making California the first US state to require the disclosures. Opponents said the laws would impose massive costs on public and private businesses, and violated the free speech protections of the US Constitution’s First Amendment.
Much of California is subject to events often associated with climate change, including wildfires, droughts, rising sea levels and temperatures well over 100 degrees Fahrenheit (38 degrees Celsius).
FIRST AMENDMENT LIMITS COMPELLED SPEECH
The appeals court unanimously said one law requiring companies with more than $500 million of annual revenue to biennially disclose climate-related risks would likely fail, because it forced companies to share "value-laden" judgments on a "politically fraught" subject rather than simply provide factual information.
It also said the other law requiring businesses with more than $1 billion of annual revenue to annually report emissions by suppliers, customers and others within their value chains went too far to address California’s interests in helping investors, reducing emissions and preventing misleading speech.
The panel said the state could have instead disseminated existing disclosures to the public, or given companies incentives to make disclosures or reduce emissions on their own.
"Climate change will increasingly affect human activity in the years ahead, forcing social, economic, and political systems to adapt to changing environmental conditions," Circuit Judge Jacqueline Nguyen, an appointee of former Democratic President Barack Obama, wrote for the court. "The First Amendment, however, limits the government’s ability to compel speech."
Defendants included officials of the California Air Resources Board and California Attorney General Rob Bonta, who enforces the state’s laws. Neither office immediately responded to requests for comment.
Daryl Joseffer, president of the US Chamber Litigation Center, in a statement called the decision an "important victory" that halted the "most onerous" disclosure requirements. He said the Chamber of Commerce will seek permanent injunctions.
TRUMP APPOINTEE PARTIALLY DISSENTS
Monday’s decision blocked California from enforcing the Climate-Related Financial Risk Act and part of the Climate Corporate Data Accountability Act, known respectively as Senate Bill 261 and Senate Bill 253.
It returned the case to US District Judge Otis Wright in Los Angeles, who had let California enforce both laws. The appeals court had last November stayed enforcement pending appeal of the financial risk law.
Circuit Judge Mark Bennett, an appointee of Republican President Donald Trump, partially dissented from Monday’s decision and would have blocked both laws.
The panel also included US District Judge Kiyo Matsumoto, an appointee of former Republican President George W. Bush who normally sits in Brooklyn, New York.

title: Supreme Court allows Trump border wall at Big Bend National Park in Texas
full_text:
By Andrew Chung
Nov 9 (Reuters) - The US Supreme Court gave President Donald Trump’s administration the green light on Monday to proceed with the construction of barriers along the US-Mexico border in a remote region in West Texas that includes Big Bend National Park, fast-tracking one of his longstanding priorities.
The court granted the administration’s emergency request to lift a federal judge’s order halting the border wall’s construction in the region while a lawsuit against the project brought by an environmental group and other challengers plays out.
The Republican president has long touted building or reinforcing barriers along the US-Mexico border as a signature part of his sweeping restrictions on immigration.
But his administration’s push to extend border infrastructure into the national park, around 250 miles (400 km) southeast of El Paso, has faced opposition from local officials, conservationists and even some Texas Republicans.
"The government’s interest," the court said in a brief ruling, "outweighs any aesthetic, recreational and environmental harm alleged by respondents."
Liberal Justice Ketanji Brown Jackson was the only member of the court, which has a 6-3 conservative majority, to publicly dissent from the decision.
The lawsuit was brought by the Center for Biological Diversity, a Big Bend-area river guide and a group seeking to preserve a historic church in Ruidosa, Texas, that says its fragile adobe structure is threatened by the border construction.
The plaintiffs challenged a series of waivers issued by the US Department of Homeland Security to expedite construction of roads and barriers in the Big Bend region, avoiding the application of a variety of environmental and conservation laws.
The waivers were issued under a 1996 federal law aimed at facilitating the construction of barriers in areas of high illegal crossings at the southern border.
In Monday’s ruling, the Supreme Court said the law at issue likely precludes judicial review of the claims brought in the lawsuit.
’HIGH ILLEGAL ENTRY’
Homeland Security Secretary Markwayne Mullin and his predecessor Kristi Noem, Trump appointees who issued the waivers between February and July, found the region to be an "area of high illegal entry," requiring additional barriers to control the border.
The administration also said that border officials have seized massive quantities of drugs in the region and that cartels operate south of the region in Mexico.
The administration said that most of the construction in the Big Bend sector, spanning more than 300 miles (480 km), will take place on privately owned land. Big Bend National Park would get a 17-mile (27-km) noncontiguous vehicle barrier system but not the kind of 30-foot (9-meter) pedestrian barrier that is slated for other areas, according to the administration.
In August, the administration paused construction in Big Bend after the project drew bipartisan criticism over its potential impact on the park’s landscape and wildlife. Crews had begun clearing land in the park for roads and border security infrastructure, prompting protests and lawsuits seeking to halt the work.
’ECOLOGICALLY AND CULTURALLY SIGNIFICANT’
Absent the waivers, the project would have to comply with numerous laws including the Endangered Species Act, the National Environmental Policy Act and the National Historic Preservation Act to alter the landscape in "one of the most remote and ecologically and culturally significant landscapes in the United States," according to the challengers.
They claimed that Mullin and Noem exceeded their authority in issuing the waivers, including by running afoul of the so-called "major questions" doctrine, which the Supreme Court has used to invalidate executive branch actions of "vast economic and political significance" unless Congress clearly authorized them.
The Supreme Court used the doctrine to stymie some of Democratic former President Joe Biden’s key executive actions, but also in February to strike down Trump’s global tariffs — a major loss for him.
In October, US District Judge Kathleen Cardone in El Paso blocked the administration’s project.
Cardone found that the waivers lacked clear congressional authorization and violated the major questions doctrine, noting that Big Bend has, by far, the lowest rate of migrant apprehensions along the entire border.
"Therefore, if the Big Bend Sector is an area of high illegal entry, so is every other sector, and the waiver authority would apply to the entire US-Mexico border," the judge said.
The Justice Department told the Supreme Court that Cardone’s ruling was baseless.
"The secretary’s waiver authority reflects a crystal-clear, indisputably valid express delegation from Congress that the executive has used for decades to expedite border-wall construction," the administration said in a filing.

title: Australia consumer sentiment sinks to 4-yr low as rate fears mount - Westpac
full_text:
Investing.com-- Australian consumer sentiment fell to its lowest level in four years in November as mounting concerns over inflation and further interest rate increases weighed on household confidence, a Westpac survey showed on Tuesday.
The Westpac-Melbourne Institute Consumer Sentiment Index dropped 2.7% to 78.2 in November from 80.4 in October, its weakest reading since late 2022. The index was down 24.6% from a year earlier.

The decline was driven by a 10.2% slump in the sub-index measuring expectations for the economy over the next 12 months, which fell to 70.3, its lowest since August 2020.
Westpac said persistent cost-of-living pressures, higher petrol prices and the Reserve Bank of Australia's latest rate increase had further undermined confidence. The RBA raised its cash rate by 25 basis points to 4.85%, an 18-year high.
Mortgage holders were particularly pessimistic, with sentiment among the group plunging 11.6% to a record low of 68.1. Meanwhile, 72% of consumers surveyed after the RBA's latest decision expected mortgage rates to rise further over the next 12 months.
The survey also showed house price expectations falling 13.4% to 99.6, the first reading below the neutral 100 mark since November 2022, while unemployment expectations rose 1.6% to 144.4.
Westpac said the deterioration in confidence pointed to mounting pressure on household spending heading into the Christmas shopping season.
